title: Soupe Kandia
author: Amina Savoura
desc: A puréed-okra stew scented with palm oil, cooked until the red oil rises back to the surface — meat, fish, crab, shrimp, dried fish and yet over white rice.
longDesc: The Afrik version is the full-dress soupou kandia: oil, yet and meat first, then onion until it turns pink, tomato concentrate, water, fresh fish, dried fish, crab, shrimp and fresh chile, and finally the okra, washed, cut and puréed. A nokoss of pounded dried chile, nététou, garlic and green onion goes in. Palm oil is added last and the stew cooks gently ‘until the red oil rises to the surface’, which is the dish’s true finish line. The page prints almost no times and no quantities for half the pot, so the stew is made by cue, not by the clock.
ingredients: A little shrimp, 4 crabs, 1 slice of smoked fish, 1 piece of yet, 1 piece of dried fish — quantities not printed for shrimp and smoked fish
1 fresh chile, dried chile (quantity not printed), nététou (quantity not printed), 3 garlic cloves, green onion (quantity not printed), onion (quantity not printed)
equipment: Blender or mortar for the okra
steps: Heat the 2 tablespoons of oil. Add the yet and the meat, and after a few moments the onion in pieces; let it turn pink.
Add the tomato concentrate and cook 3 to 4 minutes.
Add water to the pot with salt and bring to a boil to cook the meat.
Add the fresh fish, dried fish, cleaned crabs (opened), shrimp and fresh chile, then let simmer.
Wash the okra, cut and reduce it to a purée.
Make the nokoss: pound the dried chile, nététou, garlic and green onion, and add it to the pot.
Add the okra and let simmer, stirring from time to time so the sauce does not stick to the bottom.
Add the palm oil and let cook; check seasoning and cook gently until the red oil rises to the surface.
Cook the rice separately and serve the soup over white rice.
chefTips: ‘Until the red oil rises to the surface’ is the best finish cue anywhere in the soupou kandia sources — wait for it.
The nokoss of pounded chile, nététou, garlic and green onion is the same technique used in the mbakhal and in SEN012.
Stir from time to time; puréed okra and palm oil catch on the bottom.
Almost no times are printed. Cook by sight: onions pink, meat cooked, okra puréed, oil red on top.
commonMistakes: Removing the dish from the heat before the oil has risen.
reheating: Low heat, covered, with a little water.
healthBenefits: Okra supplies soluble fibre and vitamin C.
Fish and shellfish bring protein and omega-3 fats.
Palm oil is a source of vitamin E and carotenoids.
culturalNote: Soupou kandia is described in the Afrik introduction as a Senegalese staple from the Casamance that now turns up from Dakar to The Gambia. The names ‘soupe kandia’ and ‘soupou kandja’ are used interchangeably. Saveur calls the dish ‘undoubtedly a predecessor of Louisiana-style gumbo’ — a claim with no citation, recorded here as a claim.
sources: Title as printed: ‘Soupe kandia’. Byline exactly as printed: ‘Amina Savoura’. Publication: Afrik. Date as printed: ‘Publié le 15 avril 2012 à 15h54’. Yield: ‘Ingrédients (6 personnes)’. TWO-PASS; pass one verbatim, pass two paraphrased but corroborated every ingredient and every step in the same order.

Cue quoted from the introduction in a short fragment: ‘jusqu’à ce que l’huile rouge remonte en surface’. Only one time is printed in the entire method — ‘3 à 4 mn’ for the tomato. Everything else is ‘laisser mijoter’, ‘laisser bouillir’, ‘laisser cuire’ — this recipe is cue-driven, not clock-driven.
Glosses printed on the page: ‘guedj (poisson séché)’, ‘yét (mollusque séché)’, ‘nététou fermenté’. Dried fish, yet and nététou are all bought; no fermentation is performed. ‘Kecc’ does not appear.

ABSENT, not estimated: quantities for shrimp, smoked fish, dried chile, nététou, green onion, onion and salt. Printed oddities kept: ‘quelques instant’ (missing plural) and ‘les crabes ouvertes’ (feminine agreement on a masculine noun).
Cook time (90) and prep (45) are the editor’s estimate from the stage list; the page prints none.
REGIONAL ATTRIBUTION (Casamance origin, now found from Dakar to The Gambia) is SINGLE-PASS, from the Afrik introduction.
